nodes.name: Problem of non-destructive correction
nodes.statement: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems make errors. They should be corrected without damage of existing skills. The {\em problem of non-destructive correction} arises in many areas of research and development, from AI to mathematical neuroscience, where the reverse engineering of the brain ability to learn on-the-fly remains a great challenge. It is very desirable that the corrector of errors is {\em non-iterative} (one-shot) because iterative re-training of a large system requires much time and resource and cannot be done immediately without impeding activity.
nodes.statement_short: Correct the mistakes of a legacy AI system in one shot, without re-training and without damaging existing skills.

nodes.name: Extremal separability property of linear functionals in high dimension
nodes.statement: We prove that linear functionals, as learning machines, have surprising and, as far as we are concerned, new peculiar extremal properties: {\it in high dimension, with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ and for $M<a\exp(b{n})$ with $a,b>0$ every point in random i.i.d. drawn $M$-element sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is linearly separable from the rest.} Moreover, the separating linear functional can be found explicitly, without iterations. This property holds for a broad set of relevant distributions, including products of probability measures with bounded support and equidistribution in a unit ball, providing mathematical foundations for one-trial correction of legacy AI systems (cf. \citep{GorbanRomBurtTyu2016}).
nodes.statement_short: Informal statement of the paper's main result: in high dimension exponentially large random sets are point-wise linearly separable, with an explicit separating functional.
assumptions: in high dimension
with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ and for $M<a\exp(b{n})$ with $a,b>0$
random i.i.d. drawn $M$-element sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$
conclusions: every point in random i.i.d. drawn $M$-element sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is linearly separable from the rest
the separating linear functional can be found explicitly, without iterations

nodes.name: Inner product in $\Real^n$
nodes.statement: Unless stated otherwise, symbols $\boldsymbol{x}_i=(x_{i,1},\dots,x_{i,n})$ denote elements of $\Real^n$, and $\big(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j\big)=\sum_{k} x_{i,k} x_{j,k}$ is the inner product of $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_j$ in $\Real^n$.

nodes.name: Unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$
nodes.statement: Symbol $\mathbb{B}_n$ stands for the unit ball in $\Real^n$ centered at the origin: $\mathbb{B}_n=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Real^n| \ \left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\right)\leq 1\}$.

nodes.name: Linearly separable set
nodes.statement: A set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is {\em linearly separable} if for each $x\in S$ there exists a linear functional $l$ such that $l(x)>l(y)$ for all $y\in S$, $y\neq x$.
differentia: for each $x\in S$ there exists a linear functional $l$ such that $l(x)>l(y)$ for all $y\in S$, $y\neq x$

nodes.name: Extreme point of a convex compact
nodes.statement: Recall that $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is an {\em extreme point} of a convex compact $K$ if there exist no points $y,z\in K$, $y\neq z$ such that $x=(y+z)/2$.
differentia: there exist no points $y,z\in K$, $y\neq z$ such that $x=(y+z)/2$

nodes.name: Compact linearly separable sets are sets of extreme points
nodes.statement: Every compact linearly separable set $S \subset \mathbb{ R}^n$ is a set of extreme points of a convex compact $K={\rm conv} S$.
assumptions: Every compact linearly separable set $S \subset \mathbb{ R}^n$
conclusions: is a set of extreme points of a convex compact $K={\rm conv} S$

nodes.name: Proof of the proposition on compact linearly separable sets
nodes.statement: The proof follows immediately from the previous definitions, the Krein-Milman theorem \citep{Simon2011} (its finite-dimensional form was known to Minkovsky) and classical theorems about separation of a point from a convex set.
nodes.statement_short: One-line argument: combine the definitions with the Krein-Milman theorem and the classical point-from-convex-set separation theorems.

nodes.name: Simplex vertices are linearly separable and simplex volume decays as $1/n!$
nodes.statement: If $n+1$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ do not belong to a hyperplane then they are vertices of a simplex and are, obviously, linearly separable. If the lengths of the edges are bounded then the volume of the simplex decreases with $n$ not slower than $1/n!$.
assumptions: If $n+1$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ do not belong to a hyperplane
If the lengths of the edges are bounded
conclusions: they are vertices of a simplex and are, obviously, linearly separable
the volume of the simplex decreases with $n$ not slower than $1/n!$

nodes.name: Hypothesis: large random finite sets are linearly separable in high dimension
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can expect that for a sufficiently regular distribution of points, a random point does not belong to the simplex, and $n+2$ independently chosen random points are also linearly separable, with high probability, which tends to 1 as $1-c/n!$ ($n\to \infty$, $ c>0$). This fast convergence allows us to hypothesize that even a large random finite set is linearly separable in high dimension with high probability, if the distribution is regular enough. We prove this statement below for i.i.d. random points from equidistributions in a ball and a cube, and from distributions that are products of measures with bounded support.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture that large random finite sets in high dimension are linearly separable with high probability whenever the distribution is regular enough.
assumptions: for a sufficiently regular distribution of points
if the distribution is regular enough
conclusions: even a large random finite set is linearly separable in high dimension with high probability

nodes.name: Probability of a random point falling in the spherical layer $\mathbb{B}_n \setminus r\mathbb{B}_n$
nodes.statement: The probability $p$ that a random point belongs to a layer $\mathbb{B}_n \setminus r\mathbb{ B}_n$ ($0<r<1$) between spheres of radius 1 and of radius $r$ is $p=1-r^n$.
assumptions: a layer $\mathbb{B}_n \setminus r\mathbb{ B}_n$ ($0<r<1$) between spheres of radius 1 and of radius $r$

nodes.name: Upper bound on the probability that a projection exceeds $r$
nodes.statement: Let us take a unit vector $ \boldsymbol{v}$. The probability that the projection of a random vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ on $ \boldsymbol{v}$, $( \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{v})$, exceeds $r$ can be estimated from above by half of the ratio of volumes of balls of radii $\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and 1 (see Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with $\varepsilon=1-r$): $ \mathbf{P}(( \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{v})>r)\leq 0.5 \rho^{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The projection of a uniform random point of $\mathbb{B}_n$ on a fixed unit vector exceeds $r$ with probability at most $0.5\rho^n$, $\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$.
assumptions: Let us take a unit vector $ \boldsymbol{v}$
$\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$
conclusions: $ \mathbf{P}(( \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{v})>r)\leq 0.5 \rho^{n}$

nodes.name: Elementary union bound inequality
nodes.statement: an elementary inequality $\mathbf{P}(A_1 \& A_2 \& \ldots \& A_m)\geq 1- \sum_i(1-\mathbf{P}(A_i))$ for any events $A_1, \ldots , A_m$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: The proof is based on the independence of random points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$, on the geometric picture presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}, and on an elementary inequality $\mathbf{P}(A_1 \& A_2 \& \ldots \& A_m)\geq 1- \sum_i(1-\mathbf{P}(A_i))$ for any events $A_1, \ldots , A_m$. In Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} we should take $\varepsilon=1-r$ and the external radius of the spherical layer $A$ is 1.
nodes.statement_short: Combine independence with the geometric spherical-cap picture and the union bound over the $M$ events.

nodes.name: Corollary 1 (exponential sample-size estimates in the unit ball)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ and $0<r,\vartheta<1$. If \begin{equation} M<2({\vartheta-r^n})/{\rho^{n}}, \end{equation} then $ \mathbf{P}((\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_M{)}<r\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\| \mbox{ for all } i=1,\ldots, M-1)>1-\vartheta. $ If \begin{equation} M<({r}/{\rho})^n\left(-1+\sqrt{1+{2 \vartheta \rho^n}/{r^{2n}}}\right), \end{equation} then $\mathbf{P}((\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j)<r\|\boldsymbol{x}_i\| \mbox{ for all } i,j=1,\ldots, M, \, i\neq j)\geq 1-\vartheta.$ In particular, if inequality (\ref{EstimateM2ball}) holds then the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit upper bounds on $M$ guaranteeing, with probability $>1-\vartheta$, pairwise separation and hence linear separability of the whole random set in $\mathbb{B}_n$.
assumptions: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ and $0<r,\vartheta<1$
M<2({\vartheta-r^n})/{\rho^{n}}
M<({r}/{\rho})^n\left(-1+\sqrt{1+{2 \vartheta \rho^n}/{r^{2n}}}\right)

nodes.name: Weaker sufficient condition for separability in the ball
nodes.statement: A weaker and simpler estimate (sufficient condition) follows immediately from (\ref{EstimateM2ball}): \begin{equation} {\vartheta}/ M^2>{r^n+0.5\rho^{n}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Simplified sufficient condition $\vartheta/M^2 > r^n + 0.5\rho^n$ implying separability with probability $>1-\vartheta$.

nodes.name: Remark 1 (2,700,000 points in $\mathbb{R}^{100}$)
nodes.statement: According to (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) the pre exponential factor in the estimate for $M^2$ may be chosen as $\vartheta $, while the exponent depends on $r$ only. For example, for $r=1/\sqrt{2}$ the simple sufficient condition (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) gives $M^2<\frac{2}{3}\vartheta 2^{n/2}$. For $\vartheta=0.01$ (or specificity 99\%) and $n=100$ we get $M<2,740,000$. Thus, if we select 2,700,000 i.i.d. points from an equidistribution in a unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^{100} $ then with probability $p>0.99$ {\em all} these points will be vertices of their convex hull.
nodes.statement_short: Numerical instance: 2,700,000 uniform points in $\mathbb{R}^{100}$ are all vertices of their convex hull with probability $>0.99$.

nodes.name: Applicability to normalized data on a unit sphere
nodes.statement: Estimates similar to (\ref{Eq:ballMangle}), (\ref{EstimateM2ball}), and (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) are useful for the equidistribution of the normalized data on a unit sphere too. This is because they not only establish the fact of separability but also specify separation margins.

nodes.name: Product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube
nodes.statement: Consider a product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube. Let the coordinates of a random point, $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ ($0 \leq X_i \leq 1$) be independent random variables with expectations $\overline{X}_i$ and variances $\sigma_i^2>\sigma_0^2>0$. Let $\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}$ be a vector with coordinates $\overline{X}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Coordinates are independent, bounded in $[0,1]$, with variances uniformly bounded below by $\sigma_0^2$.

nodes.name: Hoeffding inequality
nodes.statement: Let $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be independent bounded random variables: $0 \leq Y_i \leq 1$. The empirical mean of these variables is defined as $\overline Y = \frac{1}{n}(Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n)$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right); \\ &\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right). \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exponential concentration of the empirical mean of independent $[0,1]$-valued variables around its expectation.
assumptions: Let $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be independent bounded random variables: $0 \leq Y_i \leq 1$
The empirical mean of these variables is defined as $\overline Y = \frac{1}{n}(Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n)$
conclusions: &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right);
&\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right).

nodes.name: Concentration radius $R$
nodes.statement: For large $n$, this distribution is concentrated in a relatively small vicinity of a sphere with an {\em arbitrary} centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ with coordinates $c_i$ and radius $R$, where \begin{equation} R^2=\mathbf{E}\left(\sum_i (X_i-c_i)^2\right)=\sum_i \sigma_i^2 + \|\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{c}\|^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The concentration radius about an arbitrary centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ splits into the total variance plus the squared offset of $\boldsymbol{c}$ from the mean.

nodes.name: Spherical layer containing a random point
nodes.statement: With probability $p>1- 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ a random point $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to the spherical layer ($\delta={nt}/{R_0^2}$, $t=\delta R_0^2/n$): \begin{equation} 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A random point lies in the relative-width-$\delta$ spherical layer around radius $R_0$ except with probability $2\exp(-2nt^2)$.

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 2 (product distribution in a unit cube)
nodes.statement: Consider a product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube. Let the coordinates of a random point, $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ ($0 \leq X_i \leq 1$) be independent random variables with expectations $\overline{X}_i$ and variances $\sigma_i^2>\sigma_0^2>0$. Let $\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}$ be a vector with coordinates $\overline{X}_i$. For large $n$, this distribution is concentrated in a relatively small vicinity of a sphere with an {\em arbitrary} centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ with coordinates $c_i$ and radius $R$, where \begin{equation} R^2=\mathbf{E}\left(\sum_i (X_i-c_i)^2\right)=\sum_i \sigma_i^2 + \|\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{c}\|^2. \end{equation} Concentration near the spheres with different centres implies concentration in the vicinity of their intersection (an example of the `waist concentration' \citep{Gromov2003}). The vicinity of the spheres, where the distribution is concentrated, can be estimated by the Hoeffding inequality \citep{Hoeffding1963}. Let $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be independent bounded random variables: $0 \leq Y_i \leq 1$. The empirical mean of these variables is defined as $\overline Y = \frac{1}{n}(Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n)$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right); \\ &\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right). \end{split} \end{equation} Let us take $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$. Consider the centres located in the cube, $0\leq c_i \leq 1$. Then $0\leq Y_i \leq 1$ and $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R^2$. In particular, if $c_i=\overline{X}_i$ then $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R_0^2$ (the minimal possible value), where $R_0^2=\sum_i \sigma_i^2\geq n\sigma_0^2$. In general, $n\sigma_0^2\leq R^2 \leq n$. With probability $p>1- 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ a random point $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to the spherical layer ($\delta={nt}/{R_0^2}$, $t=\delta R_0^2/n$): \begin{equation} 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta. \end{equation} Consider $M$ i.i.d. points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ from the product distribution. With probability $p>1- 2M\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ they all belong to the spherical layer (\ref{sphericLayer}). Therefore, with this probability we return to the situation presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with internal radius $\sqrt{1-\delta}R_0$ and external radius $\sqrt{1+\delta}R_0$. The difference from the equidistribution in the ball is that the volume of the ball is concentrated near the external sphere, while the distribution in the layer (\ref{sphericLayer}) is concentrated around the sphere $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2=R_0^2$. The radius of ball $B$ is defined by $\rho^2=(1+\delta)R_0^2-(1-\delta)R_0^2=2\delta R_0^2$. The concentration radius (\ref{ConcRad}) for the spheres concentric with the ball $B$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) is defined by $R^2=R_0^2+(1-\delta)R_0^2=(2-\delta)R_0^2$. Therefore, a random point does not belong to the ball $B$ with probability $p>1- \exp \left(-2n\tau^2 \right)$, where $\tau=\frac{1}{n}(R^2-\rho^2)=\frac{1}{n}(2-3 \delta)R^2_0$. Thus, we get the following statement.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hoeffding inequality to $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ to confine all $M$ points to a thin spherical layer, then reuse the ball geometry of Fig. 1 with radii $\sqrt{1\pm\delta}R_0$ and a union bound.

nodes.name: Set up the product distribution in the unit cube
nodes.statement: Consider a product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube. Let the coordinates of a random point, $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ ($0 \leq X_i \leq 1$) be independent random variables with expectations $\overline{X}_i$ and variances $\sigma_i^2>\sigma_0^2>0$. Let $\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}$ be a vector with coordinates $\overline{X}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the independent bounded coordinates, their means and the variance floor $\sigma_0^2$.

nodes.name: Introduce the concentration radius $R$
nodes.statement: For large $n$, this distribution is concentrated in a relatively small vicinity of a sphere with an {\em arbitrary} centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ with coordinates $c_i$ and radius $R$, where \begin{equation} R^2=\mathbf{E}\left(\sum_i (X_i-c_i)^2\right)=\sum_i \sigma_i^2 + \|\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{c}\|^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define the concentration radius about an arbitrary centre $\boldsymbol{c}$.

nodes.name: Invoke waist concentration and the Hoeffding inequality
nodes.statement: Concentration near the spheres with different centres implies concentration in the vicinity of their intersection (an example of the `waist concentration' \citep{Gromov2003}). The vicinity of the spheres, where the distribution is concentrated, can be estimated by the Hoeffding inequality \citep{Hoeffding1963}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the intersection-of-spheres concentration to an application of the Hoeffding inequality.

nodes.name: Substitute $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ and compute $\mathbf{E}[\overline Y]$
nodes.statement: Let us take $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$. Consider the centres located in the cube, $0\leq c_i \leq 1$. Then $0\leq Y_i \leq 1$ and $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R^2$. In particular, if $c_i=\overline{X}_i$ then $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R_0^2$ (the minimal possible value), where $R_0^2=\sum_i \sigma_i^2\geq n\sigma_0^2$. In general, $n\sigma_0^2\leq R^2 \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ so Hoeffding applies, giving $\mathbf{E}[\overline Y]=R^2/n$ and the bounds $n\sigma_0^2\leq R^2\leq n$.

nodes.name: Confine one random point to the spherical layer
nodes.statement: With probability $p>1- 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ a random point $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to the spherical layer ($\delta={nt}/{R_0^2}$, $t=\delta R_0^2/n$): \begin{equation} 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Turn the Hoeffding bound into membership of a single point in the relative-width-$\delta$ spherical layer.

nodes.name: Union bound over all $M$ points and reduction to the ball picture
nodes.statement: Consider $M$ i.i.d. points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ from the product distribution. With probability $p>1- 2M\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ they all belong to the spherical layer (\ref{sphericLayer}). Therefore, with this probability we return to the situation presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with internal radius $\sqrt{1-\delta}R_0$ and external radius $\sqrt{1+\delta}R_0$. The difference from the equidistribution in the ball is that the volume of the ball is concentrated near the external sphere, while the distribution in the layer (\ref{sphericLayer}) is concentrated around the sphere $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2=R_0^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the layer membership to all $M$ points by a union bound and recover the geometry of Fig. 1.

nodes.name: Compute the radius of ball $B$ and the concentric concentration radius
nodes.statement: The radius of ball $B$ is defined by $\rho^2=(1+\delta)R_0^2-(1-\delta)R_0^2=2\delta R_0^2$. The concentration radius (\ref{ConcRad}) for the spheres concentric with the ball $B$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) is defined by $R^2=R_0^2+(1-\delta)R_0^2=(2-\delta)R_0^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $\rho^2=2\delta R_0^2$ and $R^2=(2-\delta)R_0^2$ for the cap-covering ball $B$.

nodes.name: Bound the probability of falling into $B$ and conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, a random point does not belong to the ball $B$ with probability $p>1- \exp \left(-2n\tau^2 \right)$, where $\tau=\frac{1}{n}(R^2-\rho^2)=\frac{1}{n}(2-3 \delta)R^2_0$. Thus, we get the following statement.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the exponential bound $\exp(-2n\tau^2)$, $\tau=(2-3\delta)R_0^2/n$, yielding Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (separation for a product distribution in a unit cube)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points from the product distribution in a unit cube, $0< \delta <2/3$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right); \end{split} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -M(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right) \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exponential lower bounds on the probability that $M$ i.i.d. points from a bounded product distribution lie in a thin spherical layer and are pairwise separated.

nodes.name: Simplified cube estimates for $\delta=0.5$
nodes.statement: When the value of delta is chosen as $\delta=0.5$ and $R_0$ is replaced with its estimate from below, $R^2_0\geq n \sigma_0^2$, inequalities (\ref{Eq:cube1}) and (\ref{Eq:cube2}) result in the following estimates: \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq \frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1-3M\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right); \end{split} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq\frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1-M(M+1)\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right). \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Setting $\delta=0.5$ and $R_0^2\geq n\sigma_0^2$ reduces Theorem 2 to failure probabilities $3M\exp(-0.5n\sigma_0^4)$ and $M(M+1)\exp(-0.5n\sigma_0^4)$.

nodes.name: Corollary 2 (exponential sample-size estimates in the unit cube)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points from the product distribution in a unit cube and $0<\vartheta<1$. If \begin{equation} M<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right), \end{equation} then with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ \[ \begin{split} & 0.5\leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R_0^2} \leq 1.5 \mbox{ and } \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|}\right)<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ &\mbox{ for all } i,j, i \neq M. \end{split} \] If \begin{equation} (M+1)^2<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right), \end{equation} then with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ \[ \begin{split} &0.5\leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R_0^2} \leq 1.5 \mbox{ and } \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|}\right)<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ & \mbox{ for all }i,j, i\neq j. \end{split} \] In particular, if inequality (\ref{SampleSizeCube2}) holds then the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
nodes.statement_short: If $M$ (resp. $(M+1)^2$) is below $\tfrac13\vartheta\exp(0.5n\sigma_0^4)$ then the random set from the cube product distribution is linearly separable with probability $>1-\vartheta$.

nodes.name: Non-optimality and exponential dependence of the cube estimates
nodes.statement: The estimates (\ref{SampleSizeCube1}), (\ref{SampleSizeCube2}) are far from being optimal and can be improved. The main message here is their exponential dependence on $n$: the upper boundary of $M$ can grow with $n$ exponentially. Numerical experiments show that the equidistribution in cube is not worse, from the practical point of view, than the uniform distribution in a ball.

nodes.name: Numerical experiment on linear separability in unit $n$-cubes
nodes.statement: To illustrate this, we empirically assessed linear separability of samples drawn from equidistributions in the unit $n$-cubes. For selected values of $n$ from the set $\{1,\dots,5000\}$ we generated $100$ samples $S$ of $M=20 000$ random points from $[0,1]^n$. For each sample, a sub-sample $\underline{S}\subset S$ of $N=4000$ points was randomly chosen, and for each point $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ in this sub-sample linear functionals $l(\boldsymbol{x})=\left(\boldsymbol{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}},\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}}\right)-\|\boldsymbol{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}}\|^{2}$ were constructed. Sings of $l(\boldsymbol{x}_j)$, $\boldsymbol{x}_j\in S$, $\boldsymbol{x}_j\neq \boldsymbol{x}_i$ were calculated, and the numbers $N_{-}$ of instances when $l(\boldsymbol{x}_j)< 0$ where recorded. Empirical frequencies $N_{-}/N$ were then derived. Outcomes of this experiment are summarized in Fig. \ref{fig:experiments_cube}. These experiments demonstrate that the probability that a randomly selected point in a sample is linearly separable from the rest could be significantly higher than the simple exponential estimates provided. This, however, is not surprising as the estimates are based on the values of means and variances, and do not take into account other quantitative properties of the sample distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Monte-Carlo study over $n\le 5000$ with $M=20{,}000$ uniform cube points showing empirical separability frequencies well above the theoretical exponential estimates.

nodes.name: General-position separability by an additional orthogonal hyperplane
nodes.statement: In general position, a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ is linearly separable. Therefore, if $n-1$ or less points from $\mathcal{M}=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_{M-1}\}$ are not separated from $\boldsymbol{x}$ by the hyperplane $L$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) then they can be separated by an additional hyperplane orthogonal to $L$.
nodes.statement_short: At most $n-1$ leftover points can always be cut off by a second hyperplane orthogonal to the first.
assumptions: In general position
if $n-1$ or less points from $\mathcal{M}=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_{M-1}\}$ are not separated from $\boldsymbol{x}$ by the hyperplane $L$
conclusions: a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ is linearly separable
they can be separated by an additional hyperplane orthogonal to $L$

nodes.name: Two-neuron separability
nodes.statement: This means that $\boldsymbol{x}$ can be separated from the whole $\mathcal{M}$ by a conjunction of two linear inequalities, $(\bullet , \boldsymbol{x}/\|\boldsymbol{x}\|) >r \, \& \, (\bullet , \boldsymbol{y}) > q$, for some $0<r<0$, $q>0$, and $\boldsymbol{y}$, $(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})=0$. This system can be considered as a cascade of two independent neurons \citep{GorbanRomBurtTyu2016}. The probability of such a {\em two-neuron separability} is higher than of linear separability. (Compare inequality (\ref{Eq:ball1n}) in the following theorem to (\ref{Eq:ball1}).)
nodes.statement_short: Separation of a point from a set by a conjunction of two linear inequalities, i.e. a cascade of two independent neurons.
nodes.genus: separation by a conjunction of two linear inequalities
differentia: can be considered as a cascade of two independent neurons

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (cascade / two-neuron separation in the unit ball)
nodes.statement: Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$, $0<r<1$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \, \&\, \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \mbox{ points } \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \\ & \geq (1-r^n)(1-0.5\rho^{n})^{M-1} \\ &\times \left(1-\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right)^n\right) \exp{\left[\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right]}, \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on the probability that a random point of $S$ is separated from all but at most $n$ of the others, enabling a two-neuron cascade separation.

where $\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$

nodes.name: Numerical illustration of Theorem 3 for $n=100$
nodes.statement: For $r=1/\sqrt{2}$, $n=100$, and $M=2,74\cdot 10^6$, (\ref{Eq:ball1n}) gives: $\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \& \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \ \ \boldsymbol{x}_i\ \in S\right) \geq 1-\theta$ with $\theta<5\cdot 10^{-14}$. The probability stays close to $1$ for much larger values of $M$, as setting $M=7\cdot 10^{16}$ results in the estimate: $\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \& \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \ \ \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \geq 1-\theta$ with $\theta<5\cdot 10^{-9}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=100$, $r=1/\sqrt2$ the failure probability is $<5\cdot10^{-14}$ at $M=2.74\cdot10^6$ and still $<5\cdot10^{-9}$ at $M=7\cdot10^{16}$.

nodes.name: Stochastic separation theorems describe the thin structure of thin layers
nodes.statement: Classical measure concentration theorems state that random points are concentrated in a thin layer near a surface (a sphere, an average or median level set of energy or another function, etc.). The {\em stochastic separation theorems} describe thin structure of these thin layers: the random points are not only concentrated in a thin layer but are all linearly separable from the rest of the set even for exponentially large random sets. The estimates are produced for two classes of distributions in high dimension: for equidistributions in balls or ellipsoids or for the product distributions with compact support (i.e. for the case when coordinates are bounded independent random variables).
nodes.statement_short: Beyond concentration in a thin layer, the points of an exponentially large random set are all linearly separable from the rest.

nodes.name: Relax independence to weakly dependent vector-valued variables
nodes.statement: Relax the requirement of independent coordinates in Theorem~\ref{cube} to that of weakly dependent vector-valued variables;

nodes.name: Extend to strongly log-concave densities
nodes.statement: Instead of equidistributions, consider distributions with strongly log-concave probability densities;

nodes.name: Nonlinear classifiers and the role of VC dimension
nodes.statement: Use various simple and robust nonlinear classifiers like small neural cascades (compare to Theorem~\ref{CascadeSep}), algebraic classifiers and other families. For these generalisations, the VC dimension is expected to play the role similar to dimension $n$ in Theorems \ref{ball1point} and \ref{cube}.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the separation theorems to nonlinear classifier families, with VC dimension replacing $n$.

nodes.name: One-shot correction of legacy AI systems
nodes.statement: Stochastic separation Theorems 1--3 are important for synthesis and one-shot correction of AI systems. For example, inequalities (\ref{ball1point}) and (\ref{Eq:cube1}) evaluate the probability that a randomly selected point $\boldsymbol{x}_M$ is linearly separable from all other $M-1$ points by the linear functional $l(\boldsymbol{x})=(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}})$. This separation is sufficient to correct a mistake of a legacy AI system without any re-learning and modification of existing skills \citep{GorbanRomBurtTyu2016}. Such measure concentration effects reveal the hidden geometric background of the reported success of randomized neural networks models \citep{ScardapaneWang2017}.
nodes.statement_short: The explicit Fisher-type functional $l(\boldsymbol{x})=(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}})$ suffices to correct a legacy AI system's mistake without re-learning.

nodes.name: Mahalanobis inner product
nodes.statement: the Mahalanobis inner product $\langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}\rangle =(\boldsymbol{x}, S^{-1}\boldsymbol{y})$, where $S$ is the empirical covariance matrix. The Mahalanobis inner product is used for `whitening', i.e. for transformation of the data cloud into the spherical form.
nodes.origin_citation: Mahalanobis distance / whitening, classical multivariate statistics
differentia: $\langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}\rangle =(\boldsymbol{x}, S^{-1}\boldsymbol{y})$, where $S$ is the empirical covariance matrix

nodes.name: Blessing of dimensionality in data analysis
nodes.statement: Stochastic separation theorems can simplify high-dimensional data analysis and generate the 'blessing of dimensionality' \citep{GorbanTyuRom2016}. For example, according to (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}), in a dataset with 100 attributes and $M<2.7\cdot 10^6$ samples we should not be surprised to observe the linear separability of {\em each} sample from the rest of the database by the inequalities $\langle \boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j\rangle<\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\langle\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_i\rangle}$ ($i\neq j$) in the Mahalanobis inner product $\langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}\rangle =(\boldsymbol{x}, S^{-1}\boldsymbol{y})$, where $S$ is the empirical covariance matrix. The Mahalanobis inner product is used for `whitening', i.e. for transformation of the data cloud into the spherical form. Of course, these attributes should not be highly correlated and the empiric covariance matrix should be invertible.
nodes.statement_short: In a whitened 100-attribute dataset with under $2.7\cdot 10^6$ samples, each sample should be expected to be linearly separable from the rest.

nodes.name: Generalisability of corrections: separation of two random sets
nodes.statement: We analysed separation of random points from random sets. This is the problem of single {\em correction} of a legacy AI system. The question of generalisability of this correction is of great practical importance. It leads to a problem of {\em separation of two random sets}.
nodes.statement_short: How to guarantee separability of two random sets, so that a single correction generalises?

nodes.name: Quotient-space route to separating two random sets
nodes.statement: A simple series of generalisations can be immediately produced from Theorems 1-3 for separation of an $M$-element random set $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ from a $k$-element one $\{\boldsymbol{y}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{y}_k\}$ for $k<n$. For this purpose, we can consider a linear space $E=\mathrm{span}\{\boldsymbol{y}_i-\boldsymbol{y}_1 \, | \, i=2,\ldots , k\}$ and study separation of a point from an $M$-element set in the projection onto the quotient space $\mathbb{R}^{n}/E$. If ${\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_k}$ are independent then separation would likely be limited to sets of small cardinality $k<n$. If, in contrast, ${\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_k}$ are pair-wise positively correlated then we can expect that a single functional would separate them from $S$, with reasonable probability even for some $k\geq n$. This naturally gives rise to generalization of “corrections”.
nodes.statement_short: Project onto $\mathbb{R}^n/E$ to reduce separating two random sets to separating a point from a set; positive correlation among the $\boldsymbol{y}_i$ should allow $k\geq n$.

nodes.name: Grandmother cell and concept cell phenomena
nodes.statement: The reported extreme separation capabilities of linear functionals offer new insights into the Grandmother cell or concept cell phenomena that are broadly reported in neuroscience \citep{Quiroga2005}, \citep{Quiroga2009}. The essence of the phenomenon is that some neurons in the human brain respond unexpectedly selective to particular persons or objects. Strikingly, not only is the brain able to respond selectively to ``rare'' individual stimuli but also such selectivity can be learnt very rapidly from a limited number of experiences \citep{Quiroga2015}. The question is: Why small ensembles of neurons may deliver such a sophisticated functionality reliably? Stochastic separation Theorems 1-3 provide a possible answer. If we accept that a) linear functionals followed by nonlinear threshold-modulated response as phenomenological models of cells whose activity was measured, b) the number of inputs converging to these cells is large enough, and c) they are statistically independent, then extreme selectivity of responses of such models follows immediately from Theorem 2.
nodes.statement_short: Extreme selectivity of single neurons (grandmother cells) follows from Theorem 2 under linear-threshold, high-input-count and independence assumptions.
